questions.stem: A phrase differs from a clause chiefly because a phrase

options.text: is always shorter than three words
has no subject and finite verb of its own
always comes at the beginning of a sentence

questions.explanation: The defining test is grammatical, not one of length: a clause contains a subject together with a finite verb, while a phrase does not. *In the early hours of a very cold morning* is nine words long but is still only a phrase, because no subject is doing anything in it.

distractorRationale.a: Length is irrelevant — a phrase can be far longer than a short clause such as *he ran*
distractorRationale.c: Prepositional phrases are one of the commonest kinds of phrase
distractorRationale.d: Phrases occur freely at the beginning, middle or end of a sentence

questions.stem: In the sentence "The boy with the red cap won the sprint", the phrase *with the red cap* functions as

options.text: a noun phrase acting as subject

questions.explanation: The phrase tells us *which* boy won, so it describes the noun *boy*. Any phrase that describes a noun is doing an adjective's job and is therefore adjectival, whatever its internal form. In form it is a prepositional phrase; in function it is adjectival.

distractorRationale.a: An adverbial phrase would answer how, when, where or why he won, not which boy he was
distractorRationale.c: The subject is the whole noun phrase *the boy with the red cap*; the prepositional phrase alone is only part of it
distractorRationale.d: A verb phrase is built round a verb, and there is no verb inside this phrase

questions.stem: In the sentence "Racing down the slope, Musa lost control of his bicycle", the expression *Racing down the slope* is best described as

options.text: a gerund phrase acting as subject
an infinitive phrase acting as object

questions.explanation: *Racing* is a present participle, and the whole group of words built on it describes Musa — it tells us what he was doing at the time. Since there is no subject inside the group and no finite verb, it is a phrase and not a clause.

distractorRationale.b: It cannot be a clause because it contains no subject and no finite verb
distractorRationale.c: An -ing word is a gerund only when it works as a noun; here it describes a person, so it is a participle
distractorRationale.d: Infinitive phrases begin with *to* plus a verb, such as *to race down the slope*

questions.stem: In the sentence "Ngozi hopes to study medicine at Ibadan", the phrase *to study medicine at Ibadan* functions as
questions.explanation: Ask "Ngozi hopes what?" and the answer is the whole infinitive phrase, so the phrase is the object of *hopes* and is functioning as a noun. Infinitive phrases are flexible: the same phrase would be adverbial in "She travelled to Ibadan **to study medicine**", where it gives the purpose of travelling.

distractorRationale.a: There is no purpose relationship here — the phrase answers 'what', not 'why'
distractorRationale.c: The phrase does not describe Ngozi as a person; it names what she hopes for
distractorRationale.d: *Ngozi* is the subject; the phrase comes after the verb

questions.stem: In the sentence "The relief convoy arrived in the early hours of the morning", the phrase *in the early hours of the morning* is an
questions.explanation: The phrase answers the question "when did the convoy arrive?", so it modifies the verb *arrived* and is adverbial. Because the answer is a point in time rather than a location or a way of acting, it is specifically an adverbial phrase of time.

distractorRationale.b: *Hours* is a measure of time, not a location, even though the preposition *in* can also mark place
distractorRationale.c: An adjectival phrase would tell us which convoy it was
distractorRationale.d: A phrase of manner would answer 'how', such as *in great haste*

questions.stem: Identify the complete noun phrase acting as subject in the sentence "The tall boy in the blue shirt is my cousin."

options.text: The tall boy in the blue shirt

questions.explanation: A noun phrase is the head noun together with everything that modifies it, so it includes the determiner *The*, the adjective *tall* and the prepositional phrase *in the blue shirt*. The test is substitution: replace the whole group with *He* and the sentence still works, which proves the group is a single unit.

distractorRationale.a: *Boy* is only the head noun, not the whole phrase
distractorRationale.b: Stops short of the prepositional phrase, which also modifies *boy*
distractorRationale.d: This is a prepositional phrase inside the noun phrase, not the subject itself

questions.stem: In the sentence "Swimming in the Lagos lagoon is dangerous", the phrase *Swimming in the Lagos lagoon* functions as
questions.explanation: Ask "what is dangerous?" and the answer is the whole -ing phrase, so it occupies the subject position. When an -ing form works as a noun in this way it is called a gerund, and the phrase built on it is a gerund phrase acting as subject.

distractorRationale.a: Adjectival phrases modify nouns, not adjectives
distractorRationale.c: *In the Lagos lagoon* alone is a place phrase, but the question asks about the whole group
distractorRationale.d: *Dangerous* is the complement of *is*; the phrase comes before the verb

questions.stem: A phrase may contain a verb form such as a participle or an infinitive and still be a phrase rather than a clause.
questions.explanation: True. Participles and infinitives are non-finite verb forms: they show no tense and take no subject, so a group built on them remains a phrase. *Having finished the paper* and *to win the trophy* both contain verb forms, yet neither has a subject and finite verb, so neither is a clause.

questions.stem: In the sentence "Mrs Eze, a fabric trader from Onitsha, donated ten sewing machines", the phrase *a fabric trader from Onitsha* is

options.text: a noun phrase in apposition to the subject

questions.explanation: The phrase is a noun phrase placed beside another noun to identify it, set off by commas — that is apposition. Removing it leaves "Mrs Eze donated ten sewing machines", a complete sentence, which confirms that the phrase only adds information about the subject.

distractorRationale.a: *From Onitsha* is a place phrase inside the larger noun phrase, but the whole group names a person
distractorRationale.c: *Ten sewing machines* is the direct object
distractorRationale.d: It has no finite verb, so it cannot be a clause; the clause version would be *who is a fabric trader from Onitsha*

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of words is a phrase and not a clause?

options.text: at the beginning of the harmattan

questions.explanation: Only option c lacks a subject and finite verb; it is built on the preposition *at* and contains no verb at all. Each of the other three has a subject and a finite verb — *harmattan begins*, *road was*, *council repaired* — so each is a clause even though none can stand alone.

distractorRationale.a: Has the subject *the harmattan* and the finite verb *begins*, so it is an adverbial clause
distractorRationale.b: Has the subject *the road* and the finite verb *was*, so it is an adverbial clause of reason
distractorRationale.d: Has the subject *the council* and the finite verb *repaired*, so it is an adjectival clause

questions.explanation: A verb phrase consists of a main verb and its auxiliaries. The option 'running quickly' includes a verb and describes an action, making it a verb phrase.

distractorRationale.b: This is a noun phrase as it describes a subject.
distractorRationale.c: This is a prepositional phrase as it indicates a location.
distractorRationale.d: This is a noun phrase that describes a subject.
